title: Emerging Technologies Forum in New Haven focuses on AI, quantum computing

content:
NEW HAVEN, Conn. (WTNH) — About 300 technology entrepreneurs, educators, and students gathered in downtown New Haven Friday to discuss and learn about the latest emerging technologies, especially quantum computing.

“Quantum 1.0 is around us all the time in the cellphones we use, medical devices,” Southern Connecticut State University professor Christine Broadbridge, who is also the director of Research & Innovation, said. “But quantum 2.0 is about new materials, new computing that we’ve heard about, sensing and communication.”

Southern’s innovation hub hosted the Emerging Technologies Forum at 101 College St. The university is encouraging students and people of all ages to learn more about emerging technology.

“AI is affecting a lot of things today in this world in many fields,” senior nursing student Diego Flores said. “So, me, just wanting to learn a little bit more about my specific field that I’ll be going into.”

A statewide collaboration called Quantum CT is bringing two new quantum computers to New Haven, and it’s starting a business accelerator to encourage startups in the new 101 College building where the event was held.

The 100 and 101 College Street buildings were, at first, associated with the biosciences. The new quantum business accelerator moving in is not a change, but a welcome addition. Quantum computing is set to help out bioscience and lots of Connecticut industries.

“So, biotech you mentioned, advanced manufacturing, defense, finance, insurance, those are all industries that are benefiting from emerging technologies,” Broadbridge said.

So why focus on quantum computers? Because they approach problems differently.

“A classical computer is like a rat in a maze,” Quantum CT CEO Vivek Ramakrishnan explained. “For a rat to go through the maze, it has to test every point, right? And then it has to retrace. A quantum computer is like an eagle. It’s sitting on top and it can find the most efficient routes.”

That also means they need less space and power than classical computers.
